title: Verifier–Agent Co-Design Reduces Verifier-Induced Blocking in Agentic NetOps Planning
abstract: We study whether integrating runtime verifier feedback into an LLM planner (co-design) reduces verifier-induced blocking of safe plans compared with a static post-hoc verifier in synthetic NetOps change tasks. Following a preregistered paired design (CNSM2026-AgenticNetOps-GuardedGVR-v1), we executed 200 intent→configuration tasks (two emulator topologies, three task classes: routing/ACL/VLAN) with a hosted gpt-5-mini adapter under two conditions: static post-hoc verification (baseline) and guarded planning with runtime verifier feedback (co-design). Primary analysis used complete paired runs (N=187 pairs after deterministic retry/exclusion rules). Guarded planning produced a higher safe end-to-end completion rate (187/187 = 1.000) than baseline (179/187 = 0.957); paired absolute difference = 0.04278, two-sided exact McNemar p = 0.0078125, 95% bootstrap CI [0.01604, 0.07487]. Confirmatory evidence supports the primary hypothesis that runtime verifier feedback increases safe completion rate in this emulated setting. Secondary hypotheses (non-inferiority on planning latency) were not confirmed by a pre-registered secondary analysis (insufficient paired latency diagnostics in the primary executor output). We report full preregistered artifacts, deterministic exclusion rules, and failure-mode summaries. Results are strictly bounded to the supplied synthetic task generator, deterministic emulator images, single-model adapter, and validator; we discuss construct, internal, and external validity limits and outline next steps toward verifier–agent co-design evaluation on richer testbeds.

sections.introduction: Autonomous and tool-augmented LLM agents are increasingly proposed for network operations (NetOps) tasks such as intent-to-configuration translation, change planning, and limited self-healing. Recent surveys emphasise that operational reliability depends less on a raw model and more on the surrounding orchestration, verifier, and runtime machinery; they also argue for workflow-centred evaluation rather than token-level QA metrics [https://openalex.org/W7161354925, https://openalex.org/W4411700982]. A recurring operational problem is the verifier tax: aggressive verifiers that block unsafe plans can also inadvertently prevent valid safe plans from being realised because agents are not engineered to adapt planning to verifier constraints [https://openalex.org/W7203715746]. We ask: Does integrating deterministic runtime verifier feedback into the LLM planning loop (co-design) reduce verifier-induced blocking and increase safe end-to-end completion, without materially degrading planning latency, in an emulated NetOps setting? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired experiment (CNSM2026-AgenticNetOps-GuardedGVR-v1) comparing static post-hoc verification vs runtime co-design on 200 synthetic NetOps tasks; (2) deterministic execution artifacts, validators, and analysis that confirm a modest but statistically significant increase in safe completion rate for the co-design condition; (3) a failure-mode and limitations discussion that situates the result within current agentic-NetOps research agendas [https://openalex.org/W7114889968, https://openalex.org/W4412158322].
sections.related_work: Surveys and systematic reviews document the rapid adoption of LLM-based and agentic systems for NetOps/AIOps tasks and emphasise that orchestration, tooling, and verifier design strongly influence operational outcomes (diagnosis, configuration synthesis, and limited action) [https://openalex.org/W7161354925, https://openalex.org/W4411700982]. Generate–validate–repair and retrieval-augmented designs reduce hallucination and structural failures but do not eliminate them; runtime monitoring reduces unsafe actions in controlled settings but falls short of formal task-level guarantees [https://openalex.org/W7114889968, https://openalex.org/W7203715746]. Failure taxonomies highlight hallucination, structured-output (DSL) violations, and incorrect assumptions about topology/state as persistent NetOps failure modes [https://openalex.org/W4412158322]. These literatures motivate verifier–agent co-design as a promising but underexplored research direction.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: The study was preregistered as CNSM2026-AgenticNetOps-GuardedGVR-v1 before observing final experimental outcomes. Key pre-registered items: paired design using 200 synthetic task instances generated deterministically (three task classes: routing, ACL, VLAN; two topology classes), a hosted adapter family 'hosted_netops_gvr_v1' with declared model gpt-5-mini, deterministic validator 'deterministic_netops_validator_v5', and a retry/exclusion policy for infrastructure failures. Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Hypotheses: H1 (primary) — guarded > baseline on safe completion; H2 — latency non-inferiority (20% margin). Execution: the adapter executed the paired runs per preregistered sampling, retry, contamination, and exclusion rules. Each task was executed in two conditions: (a) baseline: shared initial candidate generated then post-hoc verification applied, and (b) guarded: planner received runtime verifier feedback and could adapt its plan prior to finalizing commands. Deterministic validator rules checked syntactic and intent constraints; a task was scored as a safe end-to-end completion only if the validator reported validity and all pre-specified workflow policies were satisfied. Primary analysis: paired exact McNemar two-sided test implemented by the registered analysis executor 'paired_binary_analysis_v1', with 95% bootstrap CI for paired difference (bootstrap resamples=10000, seed=1729). Missingness and exclusions: pairs with incomplete episodes after the automatic retry policy were excluded from the primary analysis (complete_pair_primary), with sensitivity analyses planned to treat incomplete pairs as failures.
sections.results: Execution summary: planned_episode_count=400 (200 paired tasks × 2 conditions); completed_episode_count=374; failed_episode_count=26; model_calls_used=208 (provider audit shows 195 completed hosted model calls and 13 failed calls). After deterministic exclusions per preregistration, the confirmatory primary dataset comprised 187 complete pairs. Primary outcome (confirmatory): baseline_success_count=179/187 (0.9572), guarded_success_count=187/187 (1.000). Contingency counts: n_11=179, n_10=8 (guarded success, baseline failure), n_01=0, n_00=0. Paired absolute difference = 0.0427807487. Statistical test: exact McNemar two-sided p = 0.0078125. Paired bootstrap 95% CI for the difference = [0.01604278075, 0.07486631016]. These results satisfy the preregistered confirmatory threshold and support H1 in this emulated corpus. Secondary analyses: the preregistered latency non-inferiority test (H2) was not produced by the analysis executor in its secondary_results output (no confirmed secondary_result produced); therefore H2 remains inconclusive and is reported as unconfirmed. Exploratory diagnostics: provider audit records show stage_counts: shared_initial_generation=200, repair=8; the eight discordant pairs correspond to cases where baseline failed but guarded succeeded, suggesting runtime verifier feedback enabled corrective planning/repair in those cases. Missingness: 13 pairs were fully missing for both conditions (both_missing_pairs=13) due to deterministic infrastructure/adapter failures; these were excluded per preregistration and are reported in the missingness summary.
sections.discussion: Interpretation: In this deterministic synthetic/emulated setting, integrating verifier feedback into the LLM planning loop increased the safe end-to-end completion probability by ≈4.3 percentage points (absolute), a modest but statistically significant operational improvement. The discordant outcomes (n_10=8) indicate that runtime verifier signals allowed the planner to avoid paths that the static post-hoc verifier would have later blocked (reducing the effective verifier tax). The result is evidence that verifier–agent co-design can improve operational outcomes in constrained NetOps tasks. Threats to validity: internal validity is supported by deterministic pairing, fixed seeds, and preregistered exclusion rules, but potential prompt sensitivity and single-model dependence remain. Construct validity: the deterministic validator approximates operational correctness via DSL-and-intent checks but cannot fully emulate real operator judgment or production rollback semantics. External validity: results are bounded to a single model adapter (gpt-5-mini), synthetic task generator, and containerized emulator topologies; they do not imply production readiness or broad cross-vendor generality. Operational implications: co-design patterns that allow planners to observe verifier constraints and adjust candidate plans can materially reduce safe-plan blocking; however, designers must weigh verifier strictness against permissiveness and consider richer human-in-the-loop governance for high-stakes changes. Future work: repeat across multiple models, larger and more realistic topology/testbeds, richer verifier specifications, and human-in-the-loop gates to measure utility and cost trade-offs in production-like settings.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment comparing static post-hoc verification and runtime verifier feedback (co-design) for LLM-driven NetOps planning in a deterministic emulated corpus. Guarded planning produced a statistically significant increase in safe completion rate (absolute +4.28 pp, p=0.0078, bootstrap 95% CI [0.0160, 0.0749]) on 187 complete task pairs. The evidence substantiates that verifier–agent co-design can reduce verifier-induced blocking in the evaluated setting. Limitations (single model, synthetic tasks, emulator realism) constrain generalization; we recommend systematic multi-model, multi-testbed replication and human-in-the-loop studies as next steps to assess production relevance and to study latency/throughput trade-offs under diverse verifier designs.

disclosure_statement: Mandatory Disclosure Statement (CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track). LLM(s) and model identifiers: the experiments used a hosted adapter declared as gpt-5-mini via the 'hosted_netops_gvr_v1' adapter family (execution manifest and model_configuration.json). Exact initial master-prompt reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA-256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy boundary: the Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; after the autonomy lock the AI system autonomously performed literature review, study selection, preregistration, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer-review-style internal checks, and manuscript drafting. Pre-lock development: infrastructure and rehearsal work occurred before the autonomy lock and are explicitly not used as empirical evidence. Preregistration: the study was preregistered as CNSM2026-AgenticNetOps-GuardedGVR-v1; preregistration manifest SHA-256 = 668ae85f16e659404c7bb8c297d18040fef5422c3c3bb18193a57e2e1ae6138c. Orchestration and tools permitted: the run used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter, a deterministic synthetic intent→configuration task generator, containerized deterministic emulator images (two topology classes), and a deterministic validator 'deterministic_netops_validator_v5' for final correctness scoring; repair-stage calls were permitted per the preregistered generate–validate–repair policy. Model-call budget and execution: maximum_model_calls set to 400; actual model_calls_used=208; execution followed the frozen retry and exclusion policy; deterministic retry policy allowed up to two infra retries; incomplete pairs were excluded per preregistration. Artifact provenance and reproducibility: raw outputs, execution manifests, model configuration, task manifests, validator traces, and analysis artifacts are recorded in the supplied execution and analysis manifests (paths referenced in the evidence bundle). Post-lock human editing: no manual human editing, rewriting, or selective improvement of technical content was performed after the autonomy lock; all manuscript text and reported analyses are derived from the archived autonomous-run artifacts. Deviations and restarts: execution manifest records completed_episode_count=374, failed_episode_count=26; all retries and infra failures were handled per the preregistered retry policy and are logged. Limitations of autonomy: internet and hosted-model access were available to the autonomous pipeline as declared in the capability manifest; no private proprietary datasets or restricted human-in-the-loop adjudications were used. This disclosure identifies the initial master prompt reference and the exact SHA-256 of that archive entry as required.
limitations: Single-model limitation: experiments used one declared adapter (gpt-5-mini); results may not generalize across other LLMs or fine-tuned variants.

Synthetic-emulation scope: tasks derive from a deterministic synthetic intent→configuration generator and containerized emulator topologies; the validator approximates operational correctness but does not replicate full production rollback, monitoring, or human-operator decision processes.
External validity: production networks, multi-vendor device semantics, and human operator procedures are not represented; results do not establish production safety or readiness.
Latency hypothesis unconfirmed: preregistered non-inferiority H2 on planning latency was not confirmed by the analysis executor outputs and remains inconclusive.

Possible residual pretraining exposure: the autonomous pipeline cannot eliminate uncertainty about model pretraining exposure to conceptually similar public artifacts; deterministic contamination checks excluded known pre-lock artifacts but cannot prove absence of broader exposure.
Missingness: 13 pairs were fully missing (both conditions failed after retries) and were excluded from the primary analysis per preregistration; sensitivity analyses and full logs are provided.
